An elective is a course or class that you choose to take — as opposed to one you are required to take.

The word "elective" comes from the idea of electing (choosing). So when something is called an elective, the central message is: this is optional; it exists by your own choice.
The Context Where You'll Meet This Word Most Often

The word "elective" as a noun lives almost entirely in educational settings — schools, colleges, and universities. Understanding it requires understanding one key contrast:

Every academic program has two kinds of courses:

  1. Required courses (also called core courses, compulsory courses, or mandatory courses): You must complete these to finish your degree or program. You have no choice in the matter. For example, a medical student must study anatomy. A law student must study contract law. These are non-negotiable.
  2. Electives: These are courses you choose to take based on your interest, curiosity, or career goals. They are not forced on you. You pick them yourself.

An elective, therefore, is a course you sign up for by your own free will, usually from a menu of available options the institution provides.

Imagine you are studying engineering at a university. Your program requires you to take Mathematics, Physics, and Computer Science. Those are your required courses — you have no choice.

But your university also says: "You must complete 3 additional courses of your choice from the following list — philosophy, economics, literature, music theory, psychology..." — those are your electives. You get to decide which ones you want.

So if you choose to take Psychology and Economics, those two courses are your electives for that semester.
How It's Used in a Sentence

• "I still have to pick an elective for next semester — I'm thinking of taking creative writing."
  • "She spent her free credits on electives in art history and film."
  • "The college requires four electives outside your major."
  • "He took philosophy as an elective even though it had nothing to do with his engineering degree."

Notice how in all of these, "elective" refers to a specific course that someone is choosing or has chosen.

"Electives" (plural) refers to the category of optional courses as a whole, or to multiple chosen courses together.

  • "This degree has 10 required courses and 5 electives."
  • "I used all my electives to explore subjects outside my major."
A Subtler Point: Choice Within Boundaries

Here is something important that many learners miss: even "electives" often involve guided choice, not completely free choice.

In many programs, you don't get to take absolutely any course in the world as your elective. Instead, the institution gives you a list of approved electives, and you choose from that list. So:

  • Free electives: You can choose any course in the entire course catalog. Total freedom.
  • Restricted electives (sometimes called track electives or stream electives): You must choose from a specific, pre-approved list. For example, "choose any 2 courses from the following 8 courses in the humanities department."

The word "elective" covers both situations. The key idea that never changes is: you are the one making the active choice — no one is forcing a specific course on you.

In medical education, the word "elective" is also used, and it follows the exact same logic. Medical students go through required clinical rotations (mandatory placements in hospitals — surgery, internal medicine, pediatrics, etc.). But they are also given time to do an elective rotation — a placement they choose based on what specialty interests them. This chosen rotation is called their "elective."

  • "She did her elective in cardiology at a hospital in London."
  • "He used his elective to explore rural medicine in a small clinic."

When someone says "I'm taking an elective," there is often a sense of personal interest, exploration, and ownership. Electives are frequently the courses students enjoy most, precisely because they chose them freely. They represent intellectual curiosity beyond what is strictly required.
An elective is a course you choose to take — it is optional and selected by you, unlike required courses that are mandatory for everyone in your program.
